source.title: FM4NPP: A Scaling Foundation Model for Nuclear and Particle Physics
source.authors: D. Park; Shu-Hang Li; Yi Huang; Xihaier Luo; Hai-Wang Yu; Yeonju Go; C. Pinkenburg; Yue-Wei Lin; Shinjae Yoo; Joseph D. Osborn; Jin Huang; Yi-Hui Ren

record.file_problem: Minor PDF text-extraction artifacts and flattened formatting; the full paper and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures scaling in a non-language scientific foundation model using validation MSE rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy, and reports downstream performance by model size.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. as related work, but those citations are not results from this study. The study's own scaling results use a simulated particle-physics dataset and MSE. Scaling-curve point values appear only in figures; the text gives qualitative trend descriptions.
record.test_reason: The study trains self-supervised Mamba2 foundation models (0.34M–188M parameters) on simulated particle-detector data, a non-language modality. It reports validation-MSE trends against model size, data size and compute (V5), and downstream performance against foundation-model size (V6). This is a new setting with its own results on the claim, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors claim validation loss follows power-law trends in model and data size, aligning with language scaling laws, with a possible saturation at m6. They say larger models overtake smaller ones as compute grows, and larger frozen FMs improve downstream performance and data efficiency on all three tasks. Their headline conclusion stresses generalization: frozen FMs with lightweight adapters beat task-specific baselines, and the representations are task-agnostic.
record.recipe_differences: Non-language particle-detector foundation model; validation MSE for a geometric self-supervised prediction task rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy. The study varies model size, dataset size, and training compute but does not fit the original language-model laws or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The model-size sweep shows a possible plateau at m6; compute comparisons vary training iteration budgets for m1–m3, while m4–m6 are trained to full completion only.

fits_no_version.finding: Pretraining gives a larger relative ARI gain over the adapter-only model with few labels than with many: 2.9× versus 1.3×.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of self-supervised pretraining over training from scratch shrinks as the amount of labeled downstream data grows.

record.problems: Scaling-curve values are provided in figures rather than transcribed in the text; uncertainty estimates for these scaling results are not stated. The tested setup is a single simulated particle-physics dataset and pretraining objective, and the largest model may be near a performance plateau.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant scaling or downstream-size outcomes were identified in the supplied text. Other downstream benchmark comparisons do not measure the versions of this claim.

untested.parts: No language models or language-model cross-entropy.
No fit on small runs is used to predict larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/data allocation is fitted.
Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
Image and video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer scaling. Fitted exponents are not reported, and no power-law fit is stated for compute scaling.
Downstream performance is not related to pretraining loss. No quantitative predictability fit.
No comparison of fitting or setup choices.

missing.what: Larger FMs consistently outperform smaller ones in track-finding ARI at every labeled-data size from 100 to 70,000. This is downstream improvement with scale across label regimes.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is a new domain and modality, not a different method on language models. All scaling evidence is figure-only and qualitative in the text, with no exponents, fits or uncertainties. Hyperparameters were tuned on m3 and transferred via µP. The model-size comparison is confounded by different iteration counts (m1–m2 at 50k, m3–m6 at 100k).

versions.untested_parts: No language models or held-out language-model cross-entropy are tested.
The study does not fit scaling laws on small runs and use them to predict much larger runs.
It does not identify a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute or fit parameter- and token-count growth against compute.
It does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at a fixed parameter count.

The study tests simulated particle-detector data with one self-supervised pretraining objective. It does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling laws, or other modalities and training regimes.
It reports downstream performance against FM size for three particle-physics tasks, but does not relate downstream performance to pretraining loss or test language-model downstream tasks.
It does not compare fitting methods, parameter-count conventions, training schedules, or data choices to determine how exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary.

rows.subject: FM4NPP (m1–m6 model-size scaling sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and measured validation mean squared error.

conditions.value: batch size 256; 50,000 iterations for m1–m2 and 100,000 for m3–m6

rows.value: figure only; text describes a clear power-law relationship and consistently decreasing validation loss with increasing parameter count, with performance plateauing at m6
rows.locator: Neural Scaling Behaviors of FM4NPP; Figure 5(a); Table 1
rows.note: The reported scaling sweep aggregates the model-size series. The authors describe a power-law trend but also note a possible saturation point at m6.
rows.check: The power-law trend is described only in words and the values are figure-only. The authors note performance plateaus at m6, a bend away from the power law at the top size. The sweep is also confounded with training length: m1–m2 got 50k iterations and m3–m6 got 100k.

rows.subject: FM4NPP (m3 data-size scaling sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Trained m3 on different-sized subsets of the training dataset and measured validation performance.
rows.value: figure only; text describes performance improving steadily with more data and following a power-law trend
rows.locator: Neural Scaling Behaviors of FM4NPP; Figure 5(b)
rows.note: The text reports the trend; individual plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: Figure-only. It covers a single 5.3M model (m3) on dataset fractions from 1% to 100%, about two orders of magnitude.

rows.subject: FM4NPP (m1–m6 compute-scaling sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation MSE against training FLOPs across models and training-iteration budgets.

conditions.value: m1–m3 trained at 25%, 50%, and 100% of their total iteration budget; m4–m6 trained to full completion only

rows.value: figure only; text says smaller models are initially more compute-efficient, while larger models outperform them when more resources are allocated
rows.locator: Neural Scaling Behaviors of FM4NPP; Figure 5(c)
rows.note: This is a qualitative compute-scaling comparison; the text does not state a power-law fit or a compute-optimal parameter/data allocation.
rows.check: The text gives no power-law fit for compute, only a qualitative crossover where smaller models are efficient early and larger models win later. The Cmin frontier appears in the figure only, so the form cannot be read. It does not bear on V3, since no allocation fit is reported.

relationships.condition: Particle-detector FM, model-size sweep m1–m5 and data-size sweep on m3
relationships.reason: Authors report a clear log-log power-law decrease in validation MSE with parameters (R1) and with data (R2). Figure-only, no exponents given.
relationships.display_finding: Validation MSE decreased in a reported power-law pattern with parameters and data, without estimated exponents.

relationships.reason: Authors state performance plateaus at m6, a possible saturation away from the power law. The size sweep also mixes 50k and 100k iteration budgets (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Performance plateaued at the 188M-parameter m6 model, while the size sweep used differing budgets of 50k and 100k iterations.

relationships.condition: Frozen FM with trained adapters on track finding, PID and noise tagging
relationships.reason: Larger pretrained models consistently yield higher performance on all three tasks (R4, R5, R6). Monotonic trend only, figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Larger pretrained models consistently performed better on all three tasks with trained adapters.
